Agile is a family of approaches to software and product development that
emerged in the early 2000s as a reaction against heavyweight, plan-driven
processes. The Agile movement is best known for a short set of values that
express what its practitioners came to prioritize over time.

At a high level, Agile values favor: individuals and interactions over rigid
processes and tooling; working software (or a working product) over
exhaustive documentation; collaborating with customers over negotiating
contract terms; and responding to change over rigidly following a plan. The
point is not that the second item in each pair has no value, but that the
first is valued more highly when the two are in tension.

They welcome changing requirements, even late in a project, treating change
as a competitive advantage rather than a disruption. They favor frequent
delivery of working results, often every few weeks. Business people and

Building a project schedule generally starts with defining the work through
a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) — decomposing the overall project into
smaller, manageable pieces down to individual tasks or work packages.

Once tasks are defined, dependencies between them are mapped. A
finish-to-start dependency, the most common type, means one task cannot
begin until another finishes. Other dependency types (start-to-start,
finish-to-finish, start-to-finish) exist but are used less frequently.

The Critical Path Method (CPM) is a widely used technique for scheduling.
It identifies the longest sequence of dependent tasks through the project —
the "critical path" — which determines the shortest possible project
duration. Any delay to a task on the critical path delays the entire
project, while

Estimating task duration is often the hardest part of scheduling. Common
approaches include analogous estimating (comparing to similar past tasks),
parametric estimating (using a rate, like hours per unit of work), and
three-point estimating, which combines optimistic, pessimistic, and most
likely estimates into a weighted average to account for uncertainty.

Once a schedule is built, it's rarely static — it should be updated
regularly as actual progress is compared against the plan, and re-baselined
when scope or timeline changes are formally approved.

text:
Risk management in a project context is the ongoing process of identifying,
assessing, and responding to uncertainties that could affect a project's
objectives — whether that's cost, schedule, scope, or quality.

Risk identification is the first step: systematically listing things that
could go wrong (threats) or unexpected opportunities that could help
(upside risks). Common techniques include brainstorming with the team,
reviewing lessons learned from past projects, and checking assumptions and
constraints for hidden fragility.

Once identified, risks are usually assessed along two dimensions: how likely
they are to occur, and how severe the impact would be if they did. Plotting
risks on a simple probability-impact grid helps teams decide which risks
deserve active attention versus which

Response strategies generally fall into a few categories. For threats: avoid
(change the plan to remove the risk entirely), mitigate (reduce the
likelihood or impact), transfer (shift the risk to a third party, such as
through insurance or a contract clause), or accept (acknowledge the risk and
do nothing further, usually because it's low priority or unavoidable). For
opportunities, the mirrored strategies are exploit, enhance, share, and
accept.

A risk register — a living document listing each risk, its assessment, its
owner, and its planned response — is a standard tool for tracking risks

text:
Scrum is a lightweight framework for managing product development work, built
around short, fixed-length iterations called sprints, typically one to four
weeks long. Each sprint aims to produce a usable increment of the product.

Three accountabilities exist in Scrum. The Product Owner is responsible for
maximizing the value of the product and manages the product backlog, an
ordered list of everything that might be needed. The Scrum Master helps the
team follow Scrum practices and removes obstacles that slow progress. The
Developers are the people who do the actual work of building the increment.

Scrum defines four core events. Sprint Planning kicks off the sprint by
deciding what can be delivered and how the work will be done. The Daily

Scrum relies on three artifacts: the Product Backlog (all known work), the
Sprint Backlog (work selected for the current sprint plus a plan to deliver
it), and the Increment (the sum of completed backlog items, tested and
potentially releasable).
